newsitem.title: USA: Albright hopeful for Israeli-Palestinian talks.
newsitem.headline: Albright hopeful for Israeli-Palestinian talks.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had a meeting on Wednesday at the White House on the Middle East and said later she was hopeful of progress in reviving Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations.
"I am hopeful this period that has been so difficult will come to an end," she said during an appearance before the Los Angeles World Affairs Council.
Albright, who is en route to Asia, said she held talks on the Middle East at the White House before departing Washington for an overnight stop in Los Angeles. She gave no details on the meeting.

In Washington, an administration official said Albright and U.S. Middle East Coordinator Dennis Ross held talks with National Security Adviser Sandy Berger. The official, who spoke anonymously, called it a routine internal session.
It was unclear how upbeat Albright meant to be in her remarks. State Department Nicholas Burns was unable to shed any light on her comments because they had not discussed the matter.
But earlier Burns indicated the United States saw no breakthrough after Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met on Tuesday in Brussels.

The Brussels meeting was "positive ... important ... a step good step forward," Burns said, but it is "not possible to give you any kind of concrete examples that it's (the peace process) moving forward."
"We still have a long way to go before we can say that significant progress is being made," he told reporters accompanying Albright to an Asian regional meeting in Malaysia.
Expectations were raised because after the Brussels talks, Levy and Arafat said they had made great strides in sweetening the bitterness of five months of acrimony over the deadlocked talks.
Neither would elaborate during a news conference on what they had agreed on to accelerate a possible return to the negotiating table but both said the meeting was a breakthrough.
But on Wednesday, the two sides toned down optimistic notes sounded a day earlier.
"Nothing was achieved yesterday," Arafat told a Brussels news conference. He renewed his call for Israel to implement fully interim peace deals signed since 1993.

A spokesman for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated a demand that the Palestinian Authority first take "real action" against "terrorist organisations outside the authority of the PA and inside it."

Albright said the United States continues to be "very concerned about the deteriorating situation in the Middle East" and she reiterated U.S. insistence that Israelis and Palestinians to "must take some of the hard decisions" needed to get the two parties back to the bargaining table.

"The Palestinians must understand the importance of security to the Israelis. The Isralies must understand the importance of not taking unilateral measures on permanent status (peace) issues," she said.
She said U.S. officials were working "hourly" on the matter and pledged that the Clinton administration would stick with its mediating role in the region.
Israeli-Palestinian talks have been deadlocked since Israel started building a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem in March, triggering Palestinian protests.
